load-context-hook.markdown: This hook builds and injects a dynamic context block into Claude's session context every time a new session starts, containing recent relationship notes, learning/wisdom readbacks, advisory findings from the last session, and a summary of active work sessions from the last 48 hours plus tracked project progress. It fires on the SessionStart event and is blocking — the session cannot proceed without its output. If it vanished, Claude would open every session with no awareness of prior conversations, unfinished work, accumulated wisdom, or relationship context, effectively starting from a blank slate each time.

load-memory-hook.markdown: Fires on every UserPromptSubmit in a primary CLI session, reads the two hot-layer memory files (PRINCIPAL_MEMORY.md and DA_MEMORY.md), and injects their entries as a `<lifeos-memory>` XML block into the prompt context. It skips subagent invocations so only the principal's own session sees the memory. Without this hook, the CLI session would be memory-blind — the autonomic loop would keep writing entries to disk but the conversation would never read them, creating a split-brain where remote channels like iMessage have full memory context while CLI turns have none. Any parse or read error silently logs to stderr and exits cleanly, so a corrupted memory file degrades to no-injection rather than blocking the prompt.

doctrine.markdown: This file is the operational core of the Algorithm — it defines the thinking loop, the ISA (Intrinsic Satisfaction Architecture) as both hill and instrument, the 16 done-claims with their HOOK/CHECK/SELF teeth, the event nudge table, and spend doctrine, all oriented toward producing euphoric surprise as the target state. It loads on the first action of any substantial run, effectively bootstrapping the entire reasoning posture before any work begins. Without it, the Algorithm has no hill to climb, no instrument to measure against, no done-claims to validate progress, and no doctrine governing when to spend or stop — the system would be directionless and unable to self-correct mid-run.

changelog.markdown: A versioned audit trail of every doctrinal change to the Algorithm, recording what shifted, why, and how to migrate or roll back between states. It loads on demand, meaning nothing in the runtime depends on it being present at execution time. If it vanished, the system would still run identically, but you'd lose your only rollback reference and the reasoning behind each doctrinal decision — making it harder to debug regressions or reverse a bad update without reconstructing intent from memory.

isasync-hook.markdown: When the model writes or edits an ISA.md file, this hook parses its frontmatter, writes the result into the work registry (work.json → Pulse board), repaints the session tab to match the derived ascent state, and spawns an HTML mirror render on completion; reads on ISA files bump a liveness heartbeat without touching the file. On any derived-state transition it injects a `<lifeos-ascent-delta>` block into the model's context carrying the authoritative phase strip, preventing the model from self-computing a status line that can drift from what the board actually shows. It fires as a PostToolUse hook scoped to ISA.md and the legacy PRD.md filename, so it is invisible to every other file operation. Without it, the work registry never receives run telemetry, tabs freeze at their initial color, the phase strip has no single source of truth, and completed runs never produce their HTML mirror — effectively severing the connection between what the model writes and what the dashboard displays.

checkpoint-hook.markdown: This hook fires whenever the agent writes or edits an ISA.md file; if it detects any claim checkbox that flipped from unchecked to checked, it iterates through an explicitly opted-in list of git repositories, stages only the files that changed during the current run, and creates one conventional commit per repo with the ISC ID and claim description as provenance. It runs event-driven on PostToolUse, is idempotent via a sidecar state file that tracks already-committed ISCs, and fails silently to avoid crashing the session. It also enforces a foreign-data boundary that refuses to stage personal transcripts or foreign-shaped paths inside the system repo, closing the gap that once caused a lifelog privacy leak. Without it, the Algorithm loses its automatic evidence trail per closed claim — you'd lose the git-log-based audit of which repository state corresponded to each ISC being marked done, and would need to commit manually or accept untracked drift.

isa-render-hook.markdown: Fires on the Stop event at end-of-turn, reads the per-session edit log written by ISASync, and spawns ISARender.ts (detached, unawaited) for each ISA that was modified during the turn. A doctrinal gate ensures renders only fire for ISAs that have already reached completion at least once, preventing constant remaking during active authoring — this is checked via an existing ISA.html or a frontmatter fallback for resumed/pre-convention ISAs. The state file is cleared after each fire, and a best-effort JSONL log records what was rendered versus skipped. Without this hook, HTML mirrors for completed ISAs would silently drift out of sync with their source artifacts after any edit, breaking downstream consumers that read the mirror rather than the ISA directly.

nudge-hook.markdown: This hook injects short one-line advisory questions into the model's context window at deterministic, pre-identified moments: when a prompt matches a skill's trigger phrase, when too many tool calls pass without an ISA edit, when a Bash command matches a destructive-infra pattern, when a known-broken capability is exercised, or when a long stretch of inline edits goes undispatched. It fires on every UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, and PostToolUseFailure event, maintaining a per-session JSON state file that tracks counters and cooldowns so no nudge repeats within its window. All nudges are advisory (the hook always exits 0 and never blocks execution), meaning the model can ignore any individual question but loses the signal if it does. Without this file, the Algorithm system loses its only real-time self-correction layer: ISAs silently go stale, subagent dispatches silently inherit the MAX rung, destructive deletes silently orphan dependent resources, and skill routing never happens because no component outside the model's own attention would notice the pattern.

verification-gate.markdown: On the Stop event it scans the assistant's final message for verification claims (deployed live, flow works, visual looks right, tests pass, version is public), then checks the transcript's actual tool calls for evidence of that work; if a blocking-type claim has no matching evidence it injects a block and forces the turn to continue rather than close. It runs every time the assistant tries to end a turn, gated by a loop guard and per-type env kill switches, and fails open on any parse error so it can never be the reason a Stop breaks. It is the mechanical teeth that prevent the assistant from closing a turn on prose alone — without it the system has no enforcement that "the login flow works" was backed by an actual browser exercise, that a deploy claim was backed by a real probe, or that a publicity claim was backed by a real public-surface check.

stop-gates.markdown: This file is the single Stop-event hook that reads stdin once and sequentially runs seven gate functions in fixed order—FormatGate, VerificationGate, ISACloseGate, ISAFoldGate, ISAGate, DeployRegistrationGate, WritingGate—emitting the first block decision it encounters and skipping all later gates after that. It fires at every turn end and always exits 0, catching per-gate crashes so a single gate failure never silences the rest or breaks the Stop event. Without it, none of the Algorithm's teeth would enforce at turn boundary: no structural format checks, no claim-vs-evidence blocks, no stale-ISA or fold-gap blocks, no deploy-registration enforcement, and no prose-quality audits would fire.

format-gate.markdown: This hook fires at Stop (after the assistant's final message is already rendered) and runs deterministic structural checks: banner on line one, closer on the last line, memory/system delta lines echoed when deltas arrived, and no more than two em-dashes in prose. It never blocks or re-emits — on violation it appends a "flag" record to `format-gate.jsonl` and returns null, because a Stop hook can only force a full re-emit which prints the response twice (the failure mode that downgraded it from a blocking gate). If this file vanished, nothing functional would break; you would simply lose the drift telemetry that keeps format violations visible so you can tune the upstream DriftReminder nudge with real data rather than guesses.

spend-auditor.markdown: At Stop, this hook reads the session transcript tail, checks whether the agent's actual capability use (skills, agents, tool calls) matched the weight of the user's ask, and if so spawns a detached, unref'd worker that runs a low-level inference pass to issue a spend verdict. It fires only when one of three triggers is met: AlgorithmNudge recorded a depth-signal this session, the session used zero Skill/Agent capability on a prompt of 200+ chars, or a work.json entry for the session just hit complete within the last 10 minutes. The hook itself is purely observational — it never blocks, never exits non-zero, and its hot path stays under 20 ms by only reading a tiny state file and spawning the worker; all heavy work (transcript parsing, inference call, JSONL writes) happens asynchronously. Verdicts append to spend-audit.jsonl, and underspend findings above 0.6 confidence also land in capability-incidents.jsonl. Without it, the system would catch depth signals at prompt time but never verify whether the agent actually delivered proportionate effort at the outcome level, leaving the zero-capability-inline failure mode unmonitored.

writing-gate.markdown: Fires on the Stop event and inspects the final response for publication signals — a `#ad`/`#sponsored` caption line, a hashtag cluster, a "here's the post" delivery phrase, or blog frontmatter — and if it finds strong signals with at least 40 words of prose, it blocks the stop unless PangramScore.ts demonstrably ran on that exact content this turn, verified by matching the SHA-256 of a deliverable block against entries logged in `pangram-runs.jsonl`. Typing a `✍️ WRITING-AUDIT:` token alone no longer satisfies the gate; only a real execution artifact does, which closes the self-attestation loophole that let a sponsored LinkedIn post ship unaudited in July 2026. It fails open on any error or when no Pangram API key is configured, degrading to telemetry-only so a fresh install with no key cannot infinite-loop on every request for a LinkedIn post. Without this hook, authored outbound prose could reach the principal's audience with no enforcement that the AI-detector audit actually happened, and the `writing-gate.jsonl` observability stream would go silent.

drift-reminder.markdown: Fires on every UserPromptSubmit with no rate limit: it reads the previous response from disk, measures it against the LifeOS format contract (banner, closer, em-dash cap, line budget, banned words), then injects a single-line FORMAT CONTRACT as additional context before the model writes the next answer — stating the allowed line count, structural rules, and exactly what the last turn broke. When the principal's prompt matches depth-request language, the line cap is lifted entirely. It replaced the old rate-limited nudge (which was silent 4 turns out of 5) and shifted enforcement from the post-write Stop hook (FormatGate, which could only block and force doubled re-emits) to a pre-write shaper, which is what actually brought daily format drift back down. Without it, the system reverts to 61-91% daily violations because no pre-generation check exists to shape output before it hits the screen.

overview.markdown:
When a message arrives, hooks (small programs at events) load memory and current state before the first token. Simple asks get a short answer; if AlgorithmNudge.hook.ts sees a depth signal, the turn becomes a run, and the model writes a definition of “done” in an ISA: a checklist of testable claims. It then works through the claims, updating the ISA as evidence arrives. Nothing is treated as complete until tools have produced evidence in the transcript, because VerificationGate.hook.ts judges claims against actual tool calls, not prose.

## Every turn — what loads before the first token and what wins conflicts.
LoadContext.hook.ts opens the session with relationship, learning, advisory findings, and active work. LoadMemory.hook.ts injects PRINCIPAL_MEMORY.md and DA_MEMORY.md on every prompt. AlgorithmNudge.hook.ts and DriftReminder.hook.ts set the event question and output contract. If sources conflict, LIFEOS/LIFEOS_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md wins; CLAUDE.md governs procedure; dynamic files report state.

## When work is real — how a run works: write done down, climb, close claims on evidence.
A real run creates or updates MEMORY/WORK/{slug}/ISA.md, or <project>/ISA.md for a persistent thing. The run climbs through ascent phases, while ISASync.hook.ts mirrors each write into MEMORY/STATE/work.json and feeds the dashboard phase strip. As claims close from [ ] to [x], CheckpointPerISC.hook.ts commits opted-in repos, leaving an evidence trail. On completion, ISARenderOnStop.hook.ts updates the HTML mirror only for ISAs that have already completed once.

## The teeth — hooks that block mechanically vs checks vs self-attestation; name the actual hook files.
StopGates.hook.ts runs the mechanical teeth at turn end. VerificationGate.hook.ts blocks claims unless the transcript shows the required tool evidence. WritingGate.hook.ts blocks publication prose unless PangramScore.ts actually ran, so a typed token no longer passes. FormatGate.hook.ts and SpendAuditor.hook.ts log checks without blocking, and AlgorithmNudge.hook.ts asks only advisory questions.

## Where the rules live — which files carry what, so the reader knows what to edit to change behavior.
Edit LIFEOS/LIFEOS_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md for constitutional behavior, CLAUDE.md for operating procedure, and its @imports for contextual knowledge. Edit LIFEOS/ALGORITHM/v{LATEST}.md to change the thinking doctrine, with history in LIFEOS/ALGORITHM/changelog.md. Edit MEMORY/WORK/{slug}/ISA.md to change a task’s definition of done. Edit hook files, settings.user.json, and checkpoint-repos.txt to change enforcement.
